feedback: If a learner ranks K-Pg as most severe, show the severity comparison: End-Permian ~90% species lost is deeper than the K-Pg toll — fame is not severity.
If a learner treats all extinctions as asteroid-caused, revisit each mechanism separately (glaciation, anoxia, volcanism, impact) so the differences stand out.
If a learner sees only destruction, direct them to the recovery phase: emptied niches let survivors diversify, as mammals did after the K-Pg.
If a learner thinks extinctions are instant, note that some unfolded over thousands to hundreds of thousands of years, and the Late Devonian over millions of years in several pulses.
activities.intendedInsight: Mass extinctions differ in cause and severity; each catastrophe both removes a large fraction of species and opens ecological space, so extinction and the later adaptive radiation, which typically took millions of years to unfold, are linked parts of the same reset-and-rediversify story.
learnerActions: Work with a biodiversity-through-time curve stretched across the geologic timeline, with the five Big Five events marked as dips.

Select an event and link it to its own kill mechanism: End-Ordovician (glaciation and sea-level fall), Late Devonian (ocean anoxia), End-Permian (Siberian Traps mega-volcanism → warming, acidification, anoxia, ~252 Mya), End-Triassic (volcanism/CAMP), K-Pg (asteroid impact).
If a dynamic model is available, trigger each mechanism and watch the diversity curve drop — deepest at the End-Permian (~90% of species) — so severity is seen, not just asserted.

For each event, move to a 'recovery' phase and watch or trace surviving groups radiate into emptied niches; after the K-Pg, follow small mammals fanning out into the niches non-avian dinosaurs left, a radiation that over tens of millions of years produced a lineage eventually including humans — a plausible consequence of the clearing, not a guaranteed one.
Use a compare-mode to overlay two events' severity and mechanism side by side and state which was more severe and why.
Write one sentence capturing the two-sided idea: a mass extinction is both an ending and a reset that enables re-diversification.
activities.title: Run the crash and the recovery on a biodiversity timeline

feedback: If a learner cannot say what radiated after an event, prompt them to connect the empty niches to the group that later diversified (e.g. mammals after K-Pg).
If severity ranking is wrong, compare the depths of the dips directly on the graph.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear comparison of dates, severities, mechanisms and recoveries can be read directly from a well-labelled curve, reinforcing that the five events differ and each is followed by diversification.
learnerActions: Examine a single annotated diversity-through-time graph with the five dips marked.
For each dip, identify its date, approximate severity (% species lost), kill mechanism, and the radiation that followed.
Mark which dip is deepest and explain why the End-Permian is deepest despite the K-Pg being better known.
Explain in your own words what 'radiated afterward' means for at least one event.
activities.title: Annotated diversity curve: read each dip

feedback: If matching errs toward one shared cause, re-separate the mechanisms.
If the K-Pg is ranked most severe, compare it to the End-Permian's ~90% loss.
Push for an explanation of WHY emptied niches enable radiation, not just naming the mammal example.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to sequence, match, rank severity and explain the extinction→radiation link demonstrates the full concept rather than isolated recall.
learnerActions: Order the Big Five chronologically with approximate dates.
Match each event to its main kill mechanism.
State which extinction was most severe (End-Permian) and justify the ranking.
Explain the extinction→radiation logic using the K-Pg→mammals→(eventually) humans chain in a written or spoken response, not just a selected option.
activities.title: Sequence, match and explain (check understanding)

feedback: If a learner claims survivors were 'the fittest/most advanced', note that survival often reflected small size, generalism or chance, not superiority.
Redirect open discussion back to the evidence: what distinguishes a 'mass' extinction (large fraction of species, short time, global driver) from background extinction.
activities.intendedInsight: Expert discussion can add depth and real-world relevance (severity drivers, the possibility of a current sixth extinction, the role of luck in survival) that complements the core comparative-causal analysis.
learnerActions: Pose questions a palaeobiologist could discuss, e.g. 'Why did roughly 90% of species die in the Great Dying?' or 'Are we entering a sixth mass extinction?'
After discussing, relate the answer back to the comparative timeline: how does this event's cause and severity sit against the others?
Consider why survivors were often small, generalist or simply lucky rather than 'the strongest or most advanced'.
activities.title: Ask a palaeobiologist (perspective extension)
